title: GitHub - skerrysoft/safeagent: Run agents in lightweight and safe VMs
excerpt: Run agents in lightweight and safe VMs. Contribute to skerrysoft/safeagent development by creating an account on GitHub.
content_html:
A lightweight Linux VM for every checkout, so parallel coding sessions can't collide, and the code they run can't reach your machine.

Coding agents like Claude Code work best in parallel: several sessions, each in its own git worktree, each on its own task. Worktrees separate the files, but everything else is shared. Two sessions both want port 3000, one branch's migration breaks the other's database, and every command an agent runs has your whole machine within reach.

safeagent gives each worktree its own small Linux VM, with its own processes, ports, Postgres, Valkey (Redis) and Temporal, and its own copy of their data. It reads what it needs from the repository (lockfiles, compose files, monorepo packages, the local addresses its env files name), so most projects need no configuration. It plugs into Claude Code, so every worktree session gets one automatically and the VM is ready in the background while the session gets on with the work; with any other tool, safeagent create makes a workspace by hand.

Two real Claude Code sessions, recorded live with asciinema (idle time trimmed to 2 s; nothing else edited). As each session opens, safeagent prepares its workspace in the background (the VM, Postgres, Temporal, npm install, migrations), shown in the status line, while Claude gets on with the code. Each has its own database: both place order #1, and only the second, which merged a branch with a new migration, has a gift_note column.

Status: early development. macOS on Apple Silicon today; Linux hosts are being built. See What works today.

Get started with Claude Code

1. Install safeagent on a Mac with Apple Silicon:

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent/releases/latest/download/safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && tar -xzf safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -C ~/.local/bin   # or anywhere on your PATH

Each release is built by GitHub Actions from this repository, with checksums (SHA256SUMS) and a signed build provenance attestation. To check a download was built here, before installing it:

gh attestation verify safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz --repo skerrysoft/safeagent

Downloaded it with a browser instead? macOS then won't run it ("cannot be opened"), as it isn't notarized yet; clear the download flag with xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/safeagent.

Or build it from source (Go 1.27+) 
git clone https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent && cd safeagent
make build                      # bin/safeagent, signed to run VMs
cp bin/safeagent ~/.local/bin/     # or anywhere on your PATH

2. Connect it to Claude Code.

safeagent claude install

This shows the three hooks it will add to ~/.claude/settings.json (WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, SessionStart), keeps a backup, and asks which folders to turn safeagent on for. safeagent only ever acts in those folders; everywhere else, worktrees stay plain worktrees.

Or use the Claude Code plugin instead

The plugin carries the same three hooks (and a small script that finds the safeagent command), and nothing else. In any Claude Code session, from any folder:

/plugin marketplace add skerrysoft/safeagent
/plugin install safeagent@safeagent

The first command adds this GitHub repository as a plugin marketplace; the second installs the plugin for your user, in every project. safeagent itself must still be installed (step 1), and it still only acts in the folders you enable (safeagent enable DIR). Use the plugin or safeagent claude install, not both: two WorktreeCreate hooks would both try to make the worktree.

3. Start sessions in worktrees, as you already do.

claude --worktree fix-login

or turn on Worktree when starting a session in the Claude desktop app. Subagents and background sessions that use worktrees work the same way.

That's all. Optionally, show each workspace in Claude Code's status line, so you can see it being prepared (add to ~/.claude/settings.json):

"statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "safeagent statusline" }

Without Claude Code (or with another agent), make a workspace yourself and work in it:

safeagent enable ~/code              # once: safeagent acts only in folders you enable
cd ~/code/shop
safeagent plan                       # what safeagent found, before anything runs
cd "$(safeagent create fix-login)"   # a worktree that gets its own VM
safeagent exec -- npm test           # the first command boots and prepares it, then runs
safeagent start                      # run the project's apps, forwarded to your machine
safeagent status                     # services, apps, and where each is on your machine

What happens in a session

  1. Claude creates the worktree through safeagent. In an enabled folder it becomes a workspace; elsewhere, a plain worktree, made the way Claude would make it.
  2. The session opens right away, and safeagent prepares the workspace in the background: builds or reuses the VM image, boots the VM (about half a second), starts the services (Postgres, Valkey, Temporal), creates the databases, installs dependencies, builds, and runs the setup you configured. The first time for a project this takes a minute or two; after that, seconds. So the database is there when you run migrations or tests.
  3. Nothing waits on that but the commands that need the VM. Claude can read and edit code and use git meanwhile. A command that needs the VM (npm test, say) waits for it, printing each step, and the status line shows where preparation has got to.
  4. Commands go to the right place automatically. node, npm, npx, yarn, pnpm and corepack run in the VM, as do the commands of any other runtime the project lists (python, go, …). Everything else, git included, runs on your machine with your keys and settings. Claude is told how the workspace works when the session starts.
  5. Your apps start when you start them, not before. Preparing a workspace never runs the project's own apps (its API, web app, workers). When your change is ready to try, run safeagent start (all of them) or safeagent start web (one, with the library watchers it needs), or ask Claude to. They run in the VM, restart if they crash, and are forwarded to your machine; safeagent stop stops them, and so does the VM stopping (safeagent down, or 30 minutes unused). Running your own dev command (npm run dev) works too: it runs in the VM like any other.
  6. Removing the worktree removes the workspace: its VM and its data. Uncommitted work and branches with commits are never deleted.

How it works

  • One VM per workspace, on Apple's Virtualization framework: a small Linux kernel (Alpine's) and a userland built from signature-verified Wolfi packages, shared read-only by every workspace that needs the same runtimes and services. It boots in about half a second.
  • Your checkout, live. The worktree is shared into the VM at the same path (virtio-fs), so your editor, git and the VM all see the same files. Dependencies install into it as Linux builds.
  • Its own disks. Service data (Postgres, Valkey) and caches (the home directory, /tmp) live on sparse disk images of the workspace's own; the rest of the system is in memory.
  • A guest agent, the VM's first process, runs the services and apps and takes commands from safeagent over SSH on vsock, with keys pinned per workspace.
  • A user-mode network. The VM's network card connects to a network stack inside safeagent (gVisor's), which lets it reach the internet and nothing local. Ports are forwarded to your machine's 127.0.0.1.
  • Sized to the project: 4 CPUs and 3 GB by default, more memory for each service and app, within half your machine.

Configure a project

Most projects need no configuration. safeagent reads the files a project already has:

Service Started when the project has… Commands in the VM get
postgres: PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector and the contrib extensions pg, postgres, pg-promise (npm); pgx, lib/pq (Go); psycopg, asyncpg (Python); pg (Ruby); a postgres/pgvector image in a compose file DATABASE_URL, PG*; database app, with vector installed
valkey: Valkey 8 (Redis-compatible) redis, ioredis, bullmq, iovalkey (npm); go-redis, valkey-go; redis (Python, Ruby); a redis/valkey image REDIS_URL, VALKEY_URL
temporal: Temporal dev server @temporalio/client or /worker; go.temporal.io/sdk; temporalio (Python); a temporalio/* image TEMPORAL_ADDRESS

It also installs dependencies from the lockfile (npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, uv sync --frozen, …), reads every package of a monorepo, gives each new workspace copies of your checkout's local .env files (so apps run as they do in your checkout), creates the local databases they point to, and builds what the apps import. safeagent itself reads env files only for local addresses, ports and variable names: every other value, and any password in a URL, is dropped as the file is read, and nothing from them is stored, printed or sent anywhere. It also finds the project's apps (packages with a dev script and a port, Procfile processes, Django's and Rails' dev servers), which safeagent start runs, with their ports forwarded to your machine; they never start on their own. safeagent plan shows all of it before anything runs, including how each app is wired: what in the VM answers at every local address its env files name, and what nothing does. To say exactly what a workspace needs, add a safeagent.yaml at the repository root:

services: [postgres, temporal]
runtimes: [python@3.12]        # Node is always there
packages: [ffmpeg]             # extra packages, by name
setup:                         # in the VM, in order, when the data is new
  - npm ci
  - npm run migrate
apps: [api, web]               # what `safeagent start` runs
ports: [3000]                  # forward another port to your machine

Setup runs once for a workspace's data, and again when its inputs change (dependencies, migrations, safeagent.yaml). The safeagent.yaml reference explains every key and exactly what runs when, in which order.

The services' variables are set for every command in the VM, so they win over the same names in a .env file (dotenv loaders don't override variables that are already set). safeagent status shows the services and the ports they are forwarded to on your machine; safeagent url postgres prints a URL, password included, for tools such as psql or a database GUI.

Working with git

The checkout is never copied into the VM. Your worktree stays an ordinary folder on your machine; the VM sees the same folder, live, at the same path, through a shared file system. Git runs on your machine, not in the VM, so it works as it always does:

  • Rebase, merge, pull, switch branches in the worktree as usual (git pull --rebase origin dev, git merge dev). The VM sees the new files the moment git writes them.
  • New dependencies or migrations arrive with a merge? The next command that runs in the VM notices (safeagent watches lockfiles, migration folders and safeagent.yaml) and runs setup again first, so the workspace installs them and migrates its own database.
  • A rebase rewrote migrations the database already ran? Start the data over: safeagent reset (back to the snapshot, if the repository has one, else empty), and setup migrates it from scratch.
  • Your editor, git GUI and Claude's file tools all work on the same files on your machine; paths in errors and stack traces match.

Code in the VM can't redirect your git: the worktree's .git pointer is locked, and repositories or Claude Code settings planted in the checkout are quarantined (see Security).

Data: seeds and snapshots

A workspace can start with real data, migrated for its own branch. A dump in the repository loads in safeagent.yaml (seed: {postgres: db/seed.sql.gz}); a dump that isn't (an anonymized copy of production, say) loads from your machine:

safeagent reset --empty && safeagent seed ~/dumps/prod.dump   # in one workspace
safeagent snapshot save                                    # make it the default

Every new workspace of the repository then starts from that snapshot (on macOS, an APFS clone: instant, and taking no space until it changes) and runs its own branch's setup on top. safeagent reset goes back to the snapshot; safeagent snapshot ls and safeagent snapshot rm NAME manage them.

Snapshots and safeagent reset cover service data only. What commands keep in the VM's home directory and /tmp (package caches, downloaded browsers, build output) lives on a second disk of the workspace's own, so it doesn't take the VM's memory; the home directory keeps it across restarts, and /tmp starts empty. It is never in a snapshot, safeagent reset leaves it, and removing the workspace deletes it.

Security

Workspaces run untrusted code: dependencies' install scripts, repository scripts, and whatever an agent decides to run. safeagent is built to contain it. Found a way out? Please report it privately, as SECURITY.md describes.

What protects you

  • VM boundary. Each workspace is a Linux VM (on macOS, Apple's Virtualization framework, which runs each VM in its own sandboxed process). It sees only its checkout, the read-only system image and its own configuration, never your machine's other files.
  • A network that only goes out. A VM's network card connects to a user-mode network stack inside safeagent, not to a bridge or your machine's network. Every connection is checked after DNS resolution: public addresses are allowed; loopback, private and link-local ranges (cloud metadata included), carrier-grade NAT, multicast, your machine's own addresses and every network it is directly attached to (VPNs included) are refused, as is outgoing mail (port 25). A VM can hold at most 512 TCP and 128 UDP flows, so it can't exhaust your machine's ports. DNS goes through your machine's resolver. Refused connections are logged (safeagent logs network).
  • Services reachable only from your machine. Forwarded ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only, at ports safeagent picks (never ones the checkout names, which could take over ports your own servers use). From your machine, Postgres and Valkey each require their own password, which other local users can't read; services without a password aren't forwarded unless you ask. The apps' web ports answer only to localhost names, so a web page can't reach them by DNS rebinding.
  • Trust inside the VM only. Inside the VM, where everything runs as root anyway, Postgres trusts the user a command names, so a project's .env URLs work unchanged (on other ports too, which relay to the service inside the VM). Connections forwarded from your machine never get that trust.
  • Clean output. What safeagent prints from the VM (logs, errors) is stripped of terminal control sequences.
  • Locked git metadata. The worktree's .git pointer is made immutable, and safeagent's own git commands name the repository explicitly, so a VM can't redirect them. After every command, at session start and every 15 seconds while a VM runs, safeagent scans the checkout for planted repositories and Claude Code settings and quarantines them.
  • Opt-in. Nothing happens outside folders you enable. Creating a worktree never runs the repository's filter drivers, or its hooks unless you opt in.
  • Pinned keys. Host and VM authenticate each other with per-workspace SSH keys that safeagent generates. Nothing is trusted on first use.
  • Verified images. Every package is checked against a signed index (Wolfi's and Alpine's pinned keys) down to each file, extraction can't write outside the image directory, and install scripts run in a build VM.
  • Careful deletion and bounded logs. safeagent only deletes worktrees it created, never a branch that holds commits, and caps the logs a VM can write on your disk.

Each of these is tested by attacking a real VM from the inside (scripts/escape-test.sh), and the parsers that read VM or repository input are fuzzed.

Known gaps

  • The checkout is shared read-write: that is how your edits reach the VM and its output reaches you. Code in the VM can change your source files, and files git tracks under .claude/. Review changes as you would any dependency's.
  • Something running in the background in a VM could plant a file between scans (up to 15 seconds).
  • No disk quota yet: a VM can fill the disk through its checkout, and its service data disk and its home disk (caches) can each grow to 64 GB. Space the VM frees is handed back to your machine.
  • The Temporal dev server and its UI have no authentication. If you forward them, any process of any user on your machine can reach them.
  • A web page served from a VM and opened in your browser is a local page: it can send requests to other services on your machine's loopback interface, as any local web app can. Open workspace apps through their *.localhost URLs.
  • A snapshot's data reaches every new workspace of its repository, whatever branch it is on, and code in those VMs can reach the internet. Don't save data in a snapshot that you wouldn't give to every branch you check out (an outside contributor's included).
  • Setup commands from safeagent.yaml, dependency installs and builds run in the VM without asking, as npm install would; the project's apps run when you (or Claude) run safeagent start.
  • Your local .env files (secrets included) are copied into each new workspace, as Claude Code's .worktreeinclude copies what it lists, so code in the VM can read them, and the VM can reach the internet. Add a .worktreeinclude to choose exactly which files a workspace gets.
  • A VM can reach anything public, from your machine's public address: code in it can send what it can read (the checkout) to the internet, and reach services that trust your IP address or a public range routed over your VPN. An allowlist mode is planned.
  • No external security review yet.

The full threat model, and the rules every change is tested against, are in docs/design.md.

Commands

You rarely need these with Claude Code; these are the ones for working by hand:

Command What it does
safeagent plan [--env] [DIR] Show what safeagent would set up for a checkout, and how its apps are wired, without starting anything
safeagent create NAME [--base BRANCH] Make a workspace (worktree on branch worktree-NAME) and print its path
safeagent start [APP…] / stop [APP…] Run or stop the project's apps in the VM (all, or the ones named); they never start on their own
safeagent status [NAME] Preparation, services, setup, whether each app answers, and where everything is on your machine
safeagent exec -- CMD… Run a command in the workspace's VM
safeagent logs [-f] WHAT A service's or an app's output, or setup, console, network
safeagent rm NAME [--force] Remove a workspace; --force discards uncommitted changes but never a branch with commits

Commands that act on a workspace use the one you're in, unless you name one.

All commands and settings
Command What it does
safeagent claude install / uninstall Add or remove the Claude Code hooks
safeagent enable [DIR] / disable [DIR], enable --list Turn safeagent on or off for a folder and everything under it
safeagent ls List workspaces
safeagent up [NAME] / down [NAME] Start (and prepare) or stop a workspace's VM
safeagent url [-w NAME] SERVICE Print a URL for a service, password included, for tools on your machine
safeagent setup [NAME] Run the project's seed and setup again
safeagent seed [-w NAME] FILE Load a .sql, .sql.gz or .dump file into the workspace's empty Postgres
safeagent snapshot save [S] / ls / rm S Save the workspace's data for new workspaces (default); list or delete snapshots
safeagent reset [NAME] [--snapshot S | --empty] Start the workspace's data over
safeagent gc Delete images and downloads no workspace needs
safeagent statusline One line for Claude Code's status line

Settings, through environment variables for now:

Variable Effect
SAFEAGENT_IDLE_STOP Stop a workspace's VM after it has been unused (no commands, no connections to its ports) this long (default 30m; off never), apps included. Its data stays; the next command starts it again, and safeagent start the apps
SAFEAGENT_CPUS, SAFEAGENT_MEMORY CPUs and memory per VM (default 4 and 3g, more memory for each service and app; at most all CPUs and half the machine's memory)
SAFEAGENT_BASE=head Start new worktrees at your current commit instead of the remote's default branch
SAFEAGENT_GIT_HOOKS=1 Let the repository's git hooks run when creating worktrees (off by default)
SAFEAGENT_BRANCH_PREFIX Prefix for new branches (default worktree-)
SAFEAGENT_FILE_EVENTS=off Don't forward file changes to watchers in the VM (by default, watchers in a VM see edits made on your machine)
SAFEAGENT_SHIMS=off Run your machine's own node, python… even in workspaces
SAFEAGENT_HOME Keep all of safeagent's state and caches under one directory

What works today
✅ Claude Code hooks: CLI, desktop app, subagents, background sessions; plugin verified
✅ One VM per workspace on macOS (Apple Silicon) ~0.5 s boot
✅ Preparation in the background, with progress in the status line and safeagent status
✅ Networking: internet yes; your machine, local network and cloud metadata no
✅ Services: Postgres 17 + pgvector, Valkey, Temporal; data kept per workspace
✅ Runtimes: Node, Python, Go, Ruby, Java, Bun, Deno; extra packages by name
✅ Dependencies installed from the lockfile; setup re-run when a merge changes them
✅ Monorepos: services, apps and library watchers detected across packages; safeagent start runs apps with forwarded ports
✅ Procfiles, Django and Rails dev servers; Python, Ruby and Go runtimes detected
✅ Local .env files copied into workspaces; the databases they name created; their secrets never read
✅ Seeds, setup commands (migrations), snapshots cloned per workspace
✅ Hot reload; idle stop; CPU and memory limits
✅ Images built only from signature-verified packages
🚧 Linux hosts in progress

Building from source

  • macOS on Apple Silicon (built and tested on macOS 27); Go 1.27+ and git
  • Network access the first time an image is built: packages come from Wolfi (packages.wolfi.dev) and the kernel from Alpine. About 100 MB, more with services and runtimes.

make build builds the guest agent for Linux, embeds it in bin/safeagent, and signs bin/safeagent with the com.apple.security.virtualization entitlement so it can start VMs. A plain go build produces a binary without the agent or the signature.

Feedback

safeagent is early. If it gets something wrong on your project (a service it missed, an app it didn't find, setup that failed), safeagent plan output in an issue helps most. Security problems go to SECURITY.md instead.

Working with git The checkout is never copied into the VM. Your worktree stays an ordinary folder on your machine; the VM sees the same folder, live, at the same path, through a shared file system. Git runs on your machine, not in the VM, so it works as it always does: Rebase, merge, pull, switch branches in the worktree as usual (git pull --rebase origin dev, git merge dev). The VM sees the new files the moment git writes them. New dependencies or migrations arrive with a merge? The next command that runs in the VM notices (safeagent watches lockfiles, migration folders and safeagent.yaml) and runs setup again first, so the workspace installs them and migrates its own database. A rebase rewrote migrations the database already ran? Start the data over: safeagent reset (back to the snapshot, if the repository has one, else empty), and setup migrates it from scratch. Your editor, git GUI and Claude's file tools all work on the same files on your machine; paths in errors and stack traces match. Code in the VM can't redirect your git: the worktree's .git pointer is locked, and repositories or Claude Code settings planted in the checkout are quarantined (see Security). Data: seeds and snapshots A workspace can start with real data, migrated for its own branch. A dump in the repository loads in safeagent.yaml (seed: {postgres: db/seed.sql.gz}); a dump that isn't (an anonymized copy of production, say) loads from your machine: safeagent reset --empty && safeagent seed ~/dumps/prod.dump # in one workspace safeagent snapshot save # make it the default Every new workspace of the repository then starts from that snapshot (on macOS, an APFS clone: instant, and taking no space until it changes) and runs its own branch's setup on top. safeagent reset goes back to the snapshot; safeagent snapshot ls and safeagent snapshot rm NAME manage them. Snapshots and safeagent reset cover service data only. What commands keep in the VM's home directory and /tmp (package caches, downloaded browsers, build output) lives on a second disk of the workspace's own, so it doesn't take the VM's memory; the home directory keeps it across restarts, and /tmp starts empty. It is never in a snapshot, safeagent reset leaves it, and removing the workspace deletes it. Security Workspaces run untrusted code: dependencies' install scripts, repository scripts, and whatever an agent decides to run. safeagent is built to contain it. Found a way out? Please report it privately, as SECURITY.md describes. What protects you VM boundary. Each workspace is a Linux VM (on macOS, Apple's Virtualization framework, which runs each VM in its own sandboxed process). It sees only its checkout, the read-only system image and its own configuration, never your machine's other files. A network that only goes out. A VM's network card connects to a user-mode network stack inside safeagent, not to a bridge or your machine's network. Every connection is checked after DNS resolution: public addresses are allowed; loopback, private and link-local ranges (cloud metadata included), carrier-grade NAT, multicast, your machine's own addresses and every network it is directly attached to (VPNs included) are refused, as is outgoing mail (port 25). A VM can hold at most 512 TCP and 128 UDP flows, so it can't exhaust your machine's ports. DNS goes through your machine's resolver. Refused connections are logged (safeagent logs network). Services reachable only from your machine. Forwarded ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only, at ports safeagent picks (never ones the checkout names, which could take over ports your own servers use). From your machine, Postgres and Valkey each require their own password, which other local users can't read; services without a password aren't forwarded unless you ask. The apps' web ports answer only to localhost names, so a web page can't reach them by DNS rebinding. Trust inside the VM only. Inside the VM, where everything runs as root anyway, Postgres trusts the user a command names, so a project's .env URLs work unchanged (on other ports too, which relay to the service inside the VM). Connections forwarded from your machine never get that trust. Clean output. What safeagent prints from the VM (logs, errors) is stripped of terminal control sequences. Locked git metadata. The worktree's .git pointer is made immutable, and safeagent's own git commands name the repository explicitly, so a VM can't redirect them. After every command, at session start and every 15 seconds while a VM runs, safeagent scans the checkout for planted repositories and Claude Code settings and quarantines them. Opt-in. Nothing happens outside folders you enable. Creating a worktree never runs the repository's filter drivers, or its hooks unless you opt in. Pinned keys. Host and VM authenticate each other with per-workspace SSH keys that safeagent generates. Nothing is trusted on first use. Verified images. Every package is checked against a signed index (Wolfi's and Alpine's pinned keys) down to each file, extraction can't write outside the image directory, and install scripts run in a build VM. Careful deletion and bounded logs. safeagent only deletes worktrees it created, never a branch that holds commits, and caps the logs a VM can write on your disk. Each of these is tested by attacking a real VM from the inside (scripts/escape-test.sh), and the parsers that read VM or repository input are fuzzed. Known gaps The checkout is shared read-write: that is how your edits reach the VM and its output reaches you. Code in the VM can change your source files, and files git tracks under .claude/. Review changes as you would any dependency's. Something running in the background in a VM could plant a file between scans (up to 15 seconds). No disk quota yet: a VM can fill the disk through its checkout, and its service data disk and its home disk (caches) can each grow to 64 GB. Space the VM frees is handed back to your machine. The Temporal dev server and its UI have no authentication. If you forward them, any process of any user on your machine can reach them. A web page served from a VM and opened in your browser is a local page: it can send requests to other services on your machine's loopback interface, as any local web app can. Open workspace apps through their *.localhost URLs. A snapshot's data reaches every new workspace of its repository, whatever branch it is on, and code in those VMs can reach the internet. Don't save data in a snapshot that you wouldn't give to every branch you check out (an outside contributor's included). Setup commands from safeagent.yaml, dependency installs and builds run in the VM without asking, as npm install would; the project's apps run when you (or Claude) run safeagent start. Your local .env files (secrets included) are copied into each new workspace, as Claude Code's .worktreeinclude copies what it lists, so code in the VM can read them, and the VM can reach the internet. Add a .worktreeinclude to choose exactly which files a workspace gets. A VM can reach anything public, from your machine's public address: code in it can send what it can read (the checkout) to the internet, and reach services that trust your IP address or a public range routed over your VPN. An allowlist mode is planned. No external security review yet. The full threat model, and the rules every change is tested against, are in docs/design.md. content_html_zh:
A lightweight Linux VM for every checkout, so parallel coding sessions can't collide, and the code they run can't reach your machine.

Coding agents like Claude Code work best in parallel: several sessions, each in its own git worktree, each on its own task. Worktrees separate the files, but everything else is shared. Two sessions both want port 3000, one branch's migration breaks the other's database, and every command an agent runs has your whole machine within reach.

safeagent gives each worktree its own small Linux VM, with its own processes, ports, Postgres, Valkey (Redis) and Temporal, and its own copy of their data. It reads what it needs from the repository (lockfiles, compose files, monorepo packages, the local addresses its env files name), so most projects need no configuration. It plugs into Claude Code, so every worktree session gets one automatically and the VM is ready in the background while the session gets on with the work; with any other tool, safeagent create makes a workspace by hand.

Two real Claude Code sessions, recorded live with asciinema (idle time trimmed to 2 s; nothing else edited). As each session opens, safeagent prepares its workspace in the background (the VM, Postgres, Temporal, npm install, migrations), shown in the status line, while Claude gets on with the code. Each has its own database: both place order #1, and only the second, which merged a branch with a new migration, has a gift_note column.

Status: early development. macOS on Apple Silicon today; Linux hosts are being built. See What works today.

Get started with Claude Code

1. Install safeagent on a Mac with Apple Silicon:

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent/releases/latest/download/safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && tar -xzf safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -C ~/.local/bin   # or anywhere on your PATH

Each release is built by GitHub Actions from this repository, with checksums (SHA256SUMS) and a signed build provenance attestation. To check a download was built here, before installing it:

gh attestation verify safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz --repo skerrysoft/safeagent

Downloaded it with a browser instead? macOS then won't run it ("cannot be opened"), as it isn't notarized yet; clear the download flag with xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/safeagent.

Or build it from source (Go 1.27+) 
git clone https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent && cd safeagent
make build                      # bin/safeagent, signed to run VMs
cp bin/safeagent ~/.local/bin/     # or anywhere on your PATH

2. Connect it to Claude Code.

safeagent claude install

This shows the three hooks it will add to ~/.claude/settings.json (WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, SessionStart), keeps a backup, and asks which folders to turn safeagent on for. safeagent only ever acts in those folders; everywhere else, worktrees stay plain worktrees.

Or use the Claude Code plugin instead

The plugin carries the same three hooks (and a small script that finds the safeagent command), and nothing else. In any Claude Code session, from any folder:

/plugin marketplace add skerrysoft/safeagent
/plugin install safeagent@safeagent

What happens in a session

  1. Claude creates the worktree through safeagent. In an enabled folder it becomes a workspace; elsewhere, a plain worktree, made the way Claude would make it.
  2. The session opens right away, and safeagent prepares the workspace in the background: builds or reuses the VM image, boots the VM (about half a second), starts the services (Postgres, Valkey, Temporal), creates the databases, installs dependencies, builds, and runs the setup you configured. The first time for a project this takes a minute or two; after that, seconds. So the database is there when you run migrations or tests.
  3. Nothing waits on that but the commands that need the VM. Claude can read and edit code and use git meanwhile. A command that needs the VM (npm test, say) waits for it, printing each step, and the status line shows where preparation has got to.
  4. Commands go to the right place automatically. node, npm, npx, yarn, pnpm and corepack run in the VM, as do the commands of any other runtime the project lists (python, go, …). Everything else, git included, runs on your machine with your keys and settings. Claude is told how the workspace works when the session starts.
  5. Your apps start when you start them, not before. Preparing a workspace never runs the project's own apps (its API, web app, workers). When your change is ready to try, run safeagent start (all of them) or safeagent start web (one, with the library watchers it needs), or ask Claude to. They run in the VM, restart if they crash, and are forwarded to your machine; safeagent stop stops them, and so does the VM stopping (safeagent down, or 30 minutes unused). Running your own dev command (npm run dev) works too: it runs in the VM like any other.
  6. Removing the worktree removes the workspace: its VM and its data. Uncommitted work and branches with commits are never deleted.

它是如何运作的

  • One VM per workspace, on Apple's Virtualization framework: a small Linux kernel (Alpine's) and a userland built from signature-verified Wolfi packages, shared read-only by every workspace that needs the same runtimes and services. It boots in about half a second.
  • Your checkout, live. The worktree is shared into the VM at the same path (virtio-fs), so your editor, git and the VM all see the same files. Dependencies install into it as Linux builds.
  • Its own disks. Service data (Postgres, Valkey) and caches (the home directory, /tmp) live on sparse disk images of the workspace's own; the rest of the system is in memory.
  • A guest agent, the VM's first process, runs the services and apps and takes commands from safeagent over SSH on vsock, with keys pinned per workspace.
  • A user-mode network. The VM's network card connects to a network stack inside safeagent (gVisor's), which lets it reach the internet and nothing local. Ports are forwarded to your machine's 127.0.0.1.
  • Sized to the project: 4 CPUs and 3 GB by default, more memory for each service and app, within half your machine.

Working with git

The checkout is never copied into the VM. Your worktree stays an ordinary folder on your machine; the VM sees the same folder, live, at the same path, through a shared file system. Git runs on your machine, not in the VM, so it works as it always does:

  • Rebase, merge, pull, switch branches in the worktree as usual (git pull --rebase origin dev, git merge dev). The VM sees the new files the moment git writes them.
  • New dependencies or migrations arrive with a merge? The next command that runs in the VM notices (safeagent watches lockfiles, migration folders and safeagent.yaml) and runs setup again first, so the workspace installs them and migrates its own database.
  • A rebase rewrote migrations the database already ran? Start the data over: safeagent reset (back to the snapshot, if the repository has one, else empty), and setup migrates it from scratch.
  • Your editor, git GUI and Claude's file tools all work on the same files on your machine; paths in errors and stack traces match.

Code in the VM can't redirect your git: the worktree's .git pointer is locked, and repositories or Claude Code settings planted in the checkout are quarantined (see Security).

Data: seeds and snapshots

A workspace can start with real data, migrated for its own branch. A dump in the repository loads in safeagent.yaml (seed: {postgres: db/seed.sql.gz}); a dump that isn't (an anonymized copy of production, say) loads from your machine:

safeagent reset --empty && safeagent seed ~/dumps/prod.dump   # in one workspace
safeagent snapshot save                                    # make it the default

Every new workspace of the repository then starts from that snapshot (on macOS, an APFS clone: instant, and taking no space until it changes) and runs its own branch's setup on top. safeagent reset goes back to the snapshot; safeagent snapshot ls and safeagent snapshot rm NAME manage them.

Snapshots and safeagent reset cover service data only. What commands keep in the VM's home directory and /tmp (package caches, downloaded browsers, build output) lives on a second disk of the workspace's own, so it doesn't take the VM's memory; the home directory keeps it across restarts, and /tmp starts empty. It is never in a snapshot, safeagent reset leaves it, and removing the workspace deletes it.

安全

Workspaces run untrusted code: dependencies' install scripts, repository scripts, and whatever an agent decides to run. safeagent is built to contain it. Found a way out? Please report it privately, as SECURITY.md describes.

What protects you

  • VM boundary. Each workspace is a Linux VM (on macOS, Apple's Virtualization framework, which runs each VM in its own sandboxed process). It sees only its checkout, the read-only system image and its own configuration, never your machine's other files.
  • A network that only goes out. A VM's network card connects to a user-mode network stack inside safeagent, not to a bridge or your machine's network. Every connection is checked after DNS resolution: public addresses are allowed; loopback, private and link-local ranges (cloud metadata included), carrier-grade NAT, multicast, your machine's own addresses and every network it is directly attached to (VPNs included) are refused, as is outgoing mail (port 25). A VM can hold at most 512 TCP and 128 UDP flows, so it can't exhaust your machine's ports. DNS goes through your machine's resolver. Refused connections are logged (safeagent logs network).
  • Services reachable only from your machine. Forwarded ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only, at ports safeagent picks (never ones the checkout names, which could take over ports your own servers use). From your machine, Postgres and Valkey each require their own password, which other local users can't read; services without a password aren't forwarded unless you ask. The apps' web ports answer only to localhost names, so a web page can't reach them by DNS rebinding.
  • Trust inside the VM only. Inside the VM, where everything runs as root anyway, Postgres trusts the user a command names, so a project's .env URLs work unchanged (on other ports too, which relay to the service inside the VM). Connections forwarded from your machine never get that trust.
  • Clean output. What safeagent prints from the VM (logs, errors) is stripped of terminal control sequences.
  • Locked git metadata. The worktree's .git pointer is made immutable, and safeagent's own git commands name the repository explicitly, so a VM can't redirect them. After every command, at session start and every 15 seconds while a VM runs, safeagent scans the checkout for planted repositories and Claude Code settings and quarantines them.
  • Opt-in. Nothing happens outside folders you enable. Creating a worktree never runs the repository's filter drivers, or its hooks unless you opt in.
  • Pinned keys. Host and VM authenticate each other with per-workspace SSH keys that safeagent generates. Nothing is trusted on first use.
  • Verified images. Every package is checked against a signed index (Wolfi's and Alpine's pinned keys) down to each file, extraction can't write outside the image directory, and install scripts run in a build VM.
  • Careful deletion and bounded logs. safeagent only deletes worktrees it created, never a branch that holds commits, and caps the logs a VM can write on your disk.

Each of these is tested by attacking a real VM from the inside (scripts/escape-test.sh), and the parsers that read VM or repository input are fuzzed.

Known gaps

  • The checkout is shared read-write: that is how your edits reach the VM and its output reaches you. Code in the VM can change your source files, and files git tracks under .claude/. Review changes as you would any dependency's.
  • Something running in the background in a VM could plant a file between scans (up to 15 seconds).
  • No disk quota yet: a VM can fill the disk through its checkout, and its service data disk and its home disk (caches) can each grow to 64 GB. Space the VM frees is handed back to your machine.
  • The Temporal dev server and its UI have no authentication. If you forward them, any process of any user on your machine can reach them.
  • A web page served from a VM and opened in your browser is a local page: it can send requests to other services on your machine's loopback interface, as any local web app can. Open workspace apps through their *.localhost URLs.
  • A snapshot's data reaches every new workspace of its repository, whatever branch it is on, and code in those VMs can reach the internet. Don't save data in a snapshot that you wouldn't give to every branch you check out (an outside contributor's included).
  • Setup commands from safeagent.yaml, dependency installs and builds run in the VM without asking, as npm install would; the project's apps run when you (or Claude) run safeagent start.
  • Your local .env files (secrets included) are copied into each new workspace, as Claude Code's .worktreeinclude copies what it lists, so code in the VM can read them, and the VM can reach the internet. Add a .worktreeinclude to choose exactly which files a workspace gets.
  • A VM can reach anything public, from your machine's public address: code in it can send what it can read (the checkout) to the internet, and reach services that trust your IP address or a public range routed over your VPN. An allowlist mode is planned.
  • No external security review yet.

The full threat model, and the rules every change is tested against, are in docs/design.md.
